finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so the authorization check is not enforced. Any request that reaches the handler can run DROP TABLE, whether or not the user has the dba role. The same line also builds the SQL by concatenating the unsanitized form value 't', which allows SQL injection (for example t=x; DROP DATABASE ...).
finding.source: HTTP request to /admin/drop from any user, including one without the dba role. The form value 't' is attacker-controlled.

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered with dropTable and has no auth middleware
userFrom(r) gets the user from the request context
Authorize(u, "dba") returns a forbidden error, but the return value is discarded
runSQL runs with the attacker-supplied table name concatenated into the statement

finding.guards_checked: The vacuum handler (api.go:33-36) checks the Authorize error and returns 403, but dropTable has no equivalent check. There is no sanitization or allowlist for 't' and no middleware on the route. userFrom (api.go:22) uses an unchecked type assertion, so a missing user in the context causes a panic (DoS) rather than an auth failure. runSQL is a stub, but the sink semantics are clear.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: Authorize (api.go:13-20) returns an error, but the call at api.go:26 is a bare statement whose result is discarded. There is no allowlist or parameterization for 't' at api.go:27, and no middleware on the route at api.go:44. The unchecked type assertion in userFrom (api.go:22) panics if no user is in the context.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 discards Authorize's error, so any caller who has a user in context reaches api.go:27, where the raw form value 't' is concatenated into DROP TABLE. The vacuum handler (api.go:33-36) shows the check that is missing. Caveat: nothing in this repo sets "user" in the context, so as written the handler panics at api.go:22 before reaching the sink. The finding therefore depends on an external auth layer that populates the context.
